To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
private physicians are more productive and use more capital per patient.
private physicians are more productive and utilize resources more efficiently.

(1) private physicians are more productive, (2) private physicians have higher levels of capital inputs per patient, (3) the effect of private ownership is not uniform across physicians, (4) skill level has the largest impact on workload, (5) referral rates have the largest impact on input utilization, and (6) the impact of private ownership is mediated by physician skill and the referral rate.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the impact of privatization on the productivity of primary care physicians.
the effects of privatization on health care providers in a transitional economy.
the effect of market forces on the productivity and resource utilization of physicians in developing countries.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
private physicians are more productive and efficient than public physicians, but that the difference is not large.

the introduction of private providers in Macedonia has had a significant effect on physician workload and capital resource use, with private providers working more hours per patient and having greater resource use per patient than their public counterparts.

the privatization of primary health care in Macedonia has resulted in a more efficient and productive system of health care provision, with private clinics exhibiting higher productivity and resource use per patient.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
private physicians are more productive than public ones.
private physicians in Macedonia do appear to work harder, but also to work more efficiently.
private physicians in Macedonia do indeed respond to market forces by increasing productivity and resource utilization.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the impact of market-based incentives on physician performance is not a foregone conclusion.
the design of health care reform in developing countries needs to be informed by empirical research that examines the impact of such reform on physician behavior and practice patterns.
, while the introduction of private clinics has increased the productivity of physicians, it has also led to a more capital intensive form of production.
